q: A microscope is an optical instrument which uses lenses to make enlarged images of objects that are too small for the unaided eye to see.
e: True. A compound microscope uses two convex lenses to enlarge a nearby tiny object. The object sits just outside the objective's focus, and total magnifying power is a product, not a sum. The objective should have the shorter focal length.

q: A compound microscope has at least two concave lenses: an objective lens and an eyepiece lens.
e: False. A compound microscope uses convex lenses, at least an objective and an eyepiece. Concave lenses diverge and will not build those real magnified images. Both stages are converging.

q: The lens nearer the object is called the objective and the lens through which the final image is viewed is called the eyepiece.
e: True. In a microscope it is short-focus and throws a real magnified image. In an astronomical telescope it is long-focus and wide for light gathering. The eyepiece is the lens toward the eye and adds angular magnification.

q: When the compound microscope is used, the object should be placed beyond $2F$, where $F$ is the focus of the objective.
e: False. For a compound microscope the object sits just outside the objective's focal point, between F and 2F, not beyond 2F. Beyond 2F you get a diminished real image, which is the wrong start. The objective must magnify.

q: The objective produces an image which is real, inverted and larger than the size of the object.
e: True. In an astronomical telescope it is long-focus and wide for light gathering. The objective is the lens toward the object. In a microscope it is short-focus and throws a real magnified image.

q: The eyepiece acts as a magnifying glass to view this image and the final image formed is virtual and on the same side as the object.
e: True. Telescope magnifying power wants this eyepiece short compared with the objective. The eyepiece is the lens toward the eye and adds angular magnification. Microscope magnifying power multiplies objective and eyepiece factors.

q: The magnifying power (MP) of a compound microscope is the sum of the magnification of the objective and the magnifying power of the eyepiece.
e: False. Magnifying power of a compound microscope is a product, M_objective times M_eyepiece, not a sum. Each stage multiplies the previous size. Adding the two numbers undercounts the enlargement.

q: For a large magnifying power of a compound microscope both the objective and the eyepiece should have short focal lengths.
e: True. The objective should have a shorter focal length than the eyepiece. A compound microscope uses at least two convex lenses to enlarge a nearby tiny object. The object sits just outside the objective's focus, and magnifying power is a product of the two stages.

q: The focal length of the objective should be longer than that of the eyepiece.
e: False. In a compound microscope the objective should have a shorter focal length than the eyepiece, so the first image is strongly magnified. A long-focus objective is the telescope choice. Microscope and telescope swap that ratio.

q: As the magnifying power increases, the sharpness of images is reduced.
e: True. magnifying and power have to stay with the same process. A different driver in place of magnifying would describe a different law.

q: Electron microscope is a microscope with high magnification and resolution, employing electron beams in place of light and using electron lenses.
e: True. Optical microscopes are the photon instruments. An electron microscope uses an electron beam and electron lenses instead of light and glass. Shorter electron wavelength gives higher magnification and resolution.

q: Optical microscopes use simple lenses, whereas electron microscopes use electrostatic or electromagnetic lenses.
e: True. Shorter electron wavelength gives higher magnification and resolution. Optical microscopes are the photon instruments. An electron microscope uses an electron beam and electron lenses instead of light and glass.

q: Optical microscopes use electrons, while electron microscopes use photons or light energy, which have shorter wavelengths that allows greater magnification.
e: False. Optical microscopes use light, photons; electron microscopes use electrons. The electron's shorter wavelength is why EM resolution is higher. The statement has the particles backwards.

q: In an electron microscope, a beam of accelerated electrons is used as a source of illumination.
e: True. Shorter electron wavelength gives higher magnification and resolution. Optical microscopes are the photon instruments. Electron microscope a beam of accelerated electrons cannot be dropped from this process without changing the law.

q: There are two main types of electron microscope: the Scanning Electron Microscope (SEM) and the Transmission Electron Microscope (TEM).
e: True. Optical microscopes are the photon instruments. An electron microscope uses an electron beam and electron lenses instead of light and glass. Two main types of electron microscope the cannot be dropped from this process without changing the law.

q: The accelerated electron beam is focused by simple glass lenses, and transmitted through the specimen.
e: False. An electron beam is focused by electron lenses, magnetic or electric, not by simple glass. Glass is for photons. The specimen still sits in the beam, but the optics are electron optics.

q: The image of the specimen may be viewed by projecting the magnified electron image onto a fluorescent viewing screen.
e: True. image and specimen have to stay with the same process. A different driver in place of image would describe a different law.
